title: Webb County Considers $1.22 Million Radio Upgrade for Responders
excerpt: Webb County is weighing a $1,216,274.58 Motorola proposal for 85 new portable radios for constables and county investigators, after Motorola told Commissioners Court that some current radios are more than 12 years past support and cannot reach rural dead zones.
content:
Webb County is considering replacing aging portable radios used by constables and county investigators, after Motorola Solutions presented a proposed upgrade to Commissioners Court on Nov. 9, according to the Laredo Morning Times. No purchase has been approved.

Motorola quoted $1,216,274.58 for an initial 85-radio package, including seven years of warranty and services, with financing options presented, according to the report.

Some of the county's current radios are more than 12 years beyond Motorola support, use a mismatched array of equipment, and operate on VHF only, while newer systems use 700/800 MHz, according to the report. Purchasing Agent Joe Lopez said the request came late in the 2026 fiscal year from the constables, the county attorney and the district attorney.

Motorola Senior Account Manager Jorge Chavez presented the APX Next system, which includes GPS, cellular fallback, Wi-Fi and over-the-air programming, according to the report. Location visibility would be limited by department, supervisor and dispatch.

Commissioners asked staff and Motorola to expand the plan beyond the initial 85 radios. The total could reach about 130 radios, including fire, the marshal, emergency management, planning, engineering, and road and bridge, according to the report. A revised price was not presented.

Precinct 4 Commissioner Ricardo Jaime cited rural dead zones, saying GPS could help dispatchers locate responders during crashes and shootings, including when a request is made for medical helicopter assistance, according to the report.

The Webb County Fire Department has already bought eight radios through recent budgets, at roughly $14,000 each, and more are still needed, according to the report.

Source: Laredo Morning Times, Nov. 16, 2026.
